en: For you indeed, O Agni, the gods, ever of one mind, have established you as the divine steward; they have established you with wisdom. They have generated the immortal among mortals through sacrifice—the godly, the wise god; they have generated every wise, godly one.
O Agni, turn Varuṇa, your brother, toward the gods with your favor—he who loves the sacrifice, the eldest who loves the sacrifice;
the Āditya who upholds the cosmic order, the king who sustains the people.

O friend, turn toward your friend, as a wheel follows the swift horse, as a chariot on its course—toward us, O wondrous one, with speed! O Agni, find favor for us with Varuṇa, and with the all-shining Maruts.
O radiant one, bestow peace upon our progeny and our strength; O wondrous one, grant us peace!
O Agni, you who are wise, may you ward off from us the wrath of the god Varuṇa;
as the best of sacrificers, the most excellent bearer of oblations, and the radiant one, release us from all hostilities.
As such, O Agni, be our protector; be our nearest helper at the dawning of this morning.
Being gracious, appease Varuṇa for us; grant us mercy and be one who is easily invoked by us.
The sight of this most fortunate god is most excellent and most wondrous among mortals;
it is like the pure, heated ghee of a cow, or like the desirable gift of the god’s bounty.
Threefold are those supreme, true, and desirable births of this divine Agni.
Enveloped within the infinite, he has come—pure, bright, noble, and resplendent.
He, the messenger, desires all dwellings; he is the Hotṛ-priest with his golden chariot and lovely tongue.
With ruddy horses, beautiful and far-shining, he is ever delightful like an assembly rich in food.
He, the kinsman of sacrifice, who brings men to awareness—him they lead forth with a great cord.
He dwells in the dwellings of this mortal man, accomplishing his task; the god has attained the state of a sharer of wealth.
May that Agni, who knows the way, lead us toward the treasure allotted by the gods which belongs to him—
that which all the immortals fashioned through their wisdom, while Dyaus, the father and begetter, poured forth the truth.
He was born first among the dwellings, at the base of the great [heaven], in the womb of this space;
footless and headless, he hid himself within the lair of the bull, drawing together the two ends.
The host has come forth first with praise, at the womb of Truth, in the lair of the Bull.
Longed-for, young, beautiful, and radiant, the seven dear ones have been born for the Steer.
Here our human fathers sat down, aspiring toward the *ṛta*;
invoking the dawns, they drove forth the cows from within the enclosure, the well-milking ones whose stall is rock, while calling upon the Dawns.
Having seen the rock, they polished it; others around them proclaimed this deed of theirs.
Guided by their cattle, they sang toward their goal; they found the light and yearned for it with their prayers.
With minds longing for cattle, the eager men, by means of their divine speech, have opened the firm, obstructed mountain that held the cows and encompassed them— the solid stall rich in cattle.

They conceived the first name of the milch-cow; they found the thrice-seven highest names of the mother. Recognizing that, the hosts of singers acclaimed her; the ruddy cow became manifest through the glory of the bull.
The evil darkness perished; the sky shone forth; the radiance of the divine Dawn has arisen.
Sūrya has mounted the vast fields, beholding both the straight and the crooked among mortals.
Then, having awakened, they looked out from behind; then indeed they took hold of the treasure allotted by heaven.
May all the gods in all their dwellings be present for our prayer; O Mitra and Varuṇa, may truth prevail!
I would call upon the brightly shining Agni, the invoker, the sustainer of all, the most excellent sacrificer;
he has pierced the pure udder like that of cows, like the purified juice of the stalk poured out.
Aditi among all those worthy of sacrifice, the guest of all human beings—
may Agni Jātavedas, choosing the protection of the gods, be gracious to us.

He who, being immortal and faithful to the *ṛta*, has been established as the god among gods and the messenger among mortals—Agni, the most excellent invoker, shall blaze forth by his greatness; he shall be impelled by the oblations of man.
O Son of Strength, born for us here today, O Agni, you move between both races of beings as our messenger,
having harnessed your lofty, straight-tailed, potent, and radiant steeds.
The two steeds that increase the strength, the ruddy ones dripping with ghee— swiftest in spirit through the Truth—
I perceive them as you yoke the ruddy horses, you travel between you gods and the clans of mortals.

Aryaman, Varuṇa, and Mitra among them, Indra and Viṣṇu, the Maruts, and the two Aśvins— O Agni, with your fine horses, fine chariot, and fine bounty, bring them hither for the person who offers the excellent oblation.
O Agni, this sacrifice is rich in cattle, rich in sheep, rich in horses, and has heroes as its friends; it is ever unassailable.
O Asura, it is provided with nourishment and progeny; it is long-lasting wealth, broad-based, and full of assembly-halls.
O Agni, for him who, sweating, brings fuel for you, or who heats his head out of devotion to you—you, being self-strong, become his protector; guard him from every malevolent one.

He who brings food to you, even when you are not seeking it, and stirs up the delightful guest—may he, the seeker of the gods, kindle you in his home; may wealth be firmly established with that generous giver.
Whoever praises you at evening or at dawn, or who, possessing oblations,
makes you his friend— he, the worshipper, like a swift horse in its own stable, you must deliver from distress.

O Agni, he who offers to you, the immortal, and performs service for you with uplifted ladle—may he, though striving, not be deprived of wealth; may no distress from the evil-minded one encompass him.

O Agni, that mortal whose well-prepared sacrifice you, the god, accept with favor, bestowing gifts— may his priestly office be pleasing to you, O youngest one, and may we be the strengtheners of him who serves you.
May the wise one distinguish between intention and lack of intention, and separate mortals according to their straight and crooked ways, like the backs of a chariot.
O God, grant us wealth with noble offspring; bestow upon us freedom and protect us from bondage.
The undeceived sages have instructed the sage, establishing him in the dwellings of the living man.
From there, O Agni, you shall behold these wondrous ones visible through your feet, by the ways of the noble one.

O Agni, most youthful one, you who provide excellent guidance to the priest who presses the Soma and serves you—O impetuous one, bring wealth to the one who exerts himself for your aid: vast, radiant, and filling the people.

And so, O Agni, whatever we have performed out of devotion to you with our feet, hands, and bodies— like those fashioning a chariot with their skillful work, the wise ones, aspiring for it, have upheld the *ṛta*.
Then may we, the seven sages, be born from the mother Dawn as the first ordainers among men;
may we become the Aṅgirases, sons of Heaven, and, shining brightly, may we shatter the mountain rich in wealth.
And just as our ancient fathers of old, O Agni, who were aspiring toward *ṛta*, went toward the pure light, chanting their hymns; cleaving the earth, they disclosed the ruddy dawns.
Performing good deeds, radiant, seeking the gods, like smiths blowing upon the birth of iron, O gods, they have come— purifying Agni, strengthening Indra, and surrounding the wide stall of cattle.
O Mighty One, you have beheld the generations of the gods like herds of cattle among a people rich in food;
even the *urvaśīs* of mortals have yearned for you, so that there may be increase for the noble one, for the sake of the future man.
We have performed service for you and become skillful workers; the radiant dawns have dawned forth as the eternal order.
They have polished Agni, who is perfect and many-colored, and the beautiful eye of the god.
O Agni, Ordainer, we have uttered these hymns for you, the Seer; accept them with favor. Blaze forth, make us more prosperous, and bestow upon us great wealth, O you who possess many boons!
Bring hither for your protection Agni, the king of the sacrifice, the Rudra, the priest of the two worlds who performs true sacrifice—
him of golden form, before the unperceived thunderbolt strikes.

This is the place of origin which we have prepared for you, as a longing wife, well-adorned, [prepares] for her husband; may you, O skillful one, sit down here, enveloped and turned toward us, facing these offerings of ours.

O worshipper, recite a hymn of praise to the immortal god who hears us, who is free from pride, who beholds men, and who is most gracious— the one whom I, like a presser of Soma, laud as the extractor of sweetness, even as the pressing-stone.

O Agni, you indeed are our *śamyā* (support) for this *ṛta*; be mindful of this *ṛta*, O wise one. When will your hymns of praise be shared in the feast? When will your friendship be realized in our home?
How indeed, O Agni, will you report that to Varuṇa? How to Heaven? What offense of ours do you reproach?
How will you speak to bountiful Mitra, to Earth? What will you say to Aryaman, what to Bhaga?

When, O Agni, will you speak from the sacrificial hearths as one who grows strong? What will you say to the powerful Vāta, who seeks splendor; what to the Nāsatyas who travel around the earth, and what, O Agni, to Rudra, the slayer of men?
How shall I speak to the great Pūṣan, the bringer of nourishment; how to Rudra, the skilled sacrificer who bestows oblations;
how to Viṣṇu, the wide-striding, regarding the seed; and how, O Agni, to the lofty arrow?
How [shall I speak] to the host of Maruts, to the Eternal Law? How, being questioned, shall I answer the great Sun?
Answer for Aditi and for the Swift One, O Jātavedas, you who are wise and perfect from heaven!
By means of *ṛta*, O Agni, I have praised the established *ṛta*: the raw cow along with the sweet, cooked [milk].
Though she is black, she has swollen with bright, life-sustaining milk.
For by the *ṛta* indeed has the bull been anointed; Agni, the manly one, with the milk of the back. Without trembling, the bestower of vigor has moved; the bright bull Pr̥śni has milked her udder.
Splitting the mountain with cosmic order (*ṛta*), the Aṅgirases shouted together with the cattle. The men sat around for good fortune at the dawn; when Agni was born, the sun became manifest.
By the cosmic order (*ṛta*), O Agni, may the immortal, unassailable goddesses, the Waters, with their honeyed floods, flow forth forever to run—
like a prize-winning steed urged on at the start of the race.

May we never go to the sacrificial station of any one who is a spirit-demon, nor of a neighbor who deceives us, nor of a kinsman; O Agni, may we not incur the debt of a crooked brother, nor may we suffer for the skill of a treacherous friend.
Protect us, O Agni, with your protections, you who are well-protecting and pleased in the sacrifice;
flash against [the foe], shatter the firm distress, and slay the *rakṣas*, even though it has grown very great.

O Agni, be well-disposed toward us through these hymns; O Hero, touch these strengths with our prayers. And, O Aṅgiras, take pleasure in our sacred formulations; may your praise, beloved by the gods, resound.
O Agni, Ordainer, I have recited all these secret songs and hidden words for you who know them— the inspired utterances and poetic wisdom— for you, the Seer, with my thoughts and hymns, O Sage.
Spread out your power like a wide net; go forth like a mighty king with his retinue.
Rushing along your swift net, you are an archer; pierce the demons with your most scorching shafts.
Your whirling flames fly swiftly; following them, touch [the enemy] boldly, O Agni, as you blaze forth.
With your tongue of fire, cast out your heats like winged insects; unfettered, scatter your firebrands in every direction.

Dispatch thy spies; be thou the swiftest one. Be thou an undeceivable guardian of this people, O Agni. Let no one who plots evil against us, whether far or near, provoke thy wrath. May no affliction from thee prevail over us.
Arise, O Agni; spread yourself out against [the foe]; burn down our enemies, O you of the sharp weapon!
O kindled one, whoever has directed hostility toward us, burn him down like dry brushwood.
Stand upright and pierce them; O Agni, manifest your divine powers against us.
Slacken the firm bows of those driven by demons; crush our enemies, whether they be kin or strangers.
O Most Youthful One, he knows your benevolence who has prepared a path for this sacred prayer;
for him, you have shone light upon all auspicious days, upon the riches of the noble one, and upon his glories, opening wide the doors.

O Agni, let him be fortunate and a liberal giver who, throughout his own life and within his home, desires to satisfy you with constant oblations and hymns; for him, may every sacrifice result in auspicious days.
I praise your benevolence; let my voice be heard nearby. May this song of mine resound for you like a beloved wife.
O you who possess fine horses and beautiful chariots, may we adorn you; may you maintain sovereign powers for us day after day.
May many a person come here to you of their own accord, O dispeller of darkness, as you shine day after day;
may we, joyful and playing, serve you, while we stand amidst the splendors of the people.
O Agni, for him who approaches you with good horses and fine gold on a chariot laden with wealth—
you become his protector and his friend, he who continually delights in showing you hospitality.

Through my kinship and with my words, I shatter the great [fortresses]. This has come down to me from my father Gotama. O most youthful Hotṛ, wise one, master of the house, take heed of this our speech.
Sleepless, swift-crossing, most gracious, unwearied, free from predators, and most tireless—
may those guardians of yours, O Agni, sitting together in harmony, protect us, O wise one.

Those protectors of yours, O Agni, who, seeing him blind, preserved Māmateya from misfortune—they, the all-knowing one, have protected those doers of good; though the enemies sought to deceive them, they did not succeed in deceiving.
Through you may we be successful; protected by you, under your guidance, may we obtain spoils of war.
Accomplish both our prayers, O upholder of truth; act with immediate efficacy, O fearless one.
With this fuel, O Agni, may we worship you; accept the hymn of praise being recited.
Burn away the devouring Rākṣasas; protect us from malice, from reproach, and from blame, O you who are great as Mitra.
In unison with the bountiful Vaiśvānara, how shall we offer great light to Agni?
With his perfect and lofty growth, he has propped up the firmament like a supporting pillar.

Do not revile him who, as a god, has bestowed this gift upon me, a mortal— Agni Vaiśvānara, the wise, the immortal, the discerning, the most manly, the youthful, and the skillful one, for the sake of the simple-minded.
The Sāman-dwelling one, doubly great, with sharp-pointed horns, thousandfold-seeded and powerful bull—
having found the hidden track of the cow like Agni, he has proclaimed to me this inspired thought.
May Agni, the bounteous giver, with his sharp-jawed flame and most fervent glow,
consume those who violate the ordinances of Varuṇa and the beloved, steadfast laws of the mindful Mitra.
Like brotherless maidens wandering abroad, like wives of enemies who are ill-disposed,
being wicked, false, and untruthful, they have produced this deep place.
O Agni, Purifier, upon me—though I am so small and unwise—you have boldly placed this great, profound, and mighty hymn, like a heavy burden; it is a sevenfold back, rich with sacrificial food.
May our purifying prayer, through its wisdom, reach him who is common to all and equal to all;
may it reach that lovely, youthful form fashioned upon the skin of the plant, upon the summit of the speckled earth.
What of this speech of mine is to be proclaimed? They speak of that which is hidden in the secret cave.
When they have uncovered the cows like a flood of water, he guards the beloved summit of the form, the footstep of the bird.
And this indeed was that great, mighty array, which the ancient cow, the ruddy one, accompanied;
shining in the station of Order, he found it hidden away, moving swiftly, hastening on.
Then, shining while dwelling with his parents, he recognized the secret, lovely [form] of Pṛśni;
in the highest station of the mother, near the cow, was the tongue of the extended, virile flame.
Being questioned, I speak the truth with reverence and with hope for you, O Jātavedas, regarding all this that exists here:
you rule over all that wealth which is in heaven and that which is upon the earth.
What wealth of his is ours, and what treasure? O Jātavedas, you who are wise, declare it to us.
For we have gone to the highest point of this secret path, like a trackless footstep, without a firm foundation.

What is the boundary, what are the rules? When shall we reach your favor, like swift horses reaching for the prize? When will the goddesses, the wives of the Immortal, extend over us with the splendor of the Sun, O Dawns?
With speech that is not refined, feeble, dependent, and insignificant, they are not satisfied.
Therefore, O Agni, what do they say here to you? Let those who are unarmed be joined with falsehood.
For the glory of this kindled bull, the face of the Vasu has shone forth within the house.
Clothed in brilliance, beautiful in form, he has gleamed like a dwelling with wealth—much-desired and worthy of praise.
Stand up erect for us, O Agni, Hotṛ-priest of the sacrifice, most skilled in worship among the gods;
for you indeed surpass every thought, and you further even the inspired wisdom of the wise.
The unerring Hotṛ has been seated among the people—Agni, the delightful one, wise in the assemblies.
Like Sūrya, he has extended his light upward; like a pillar, he supports the smoke toward heaven.
As the well-warmed, bountiful ladle, dripping with ghee, moves to the right, choosing the assembly of the gods,
the sacrificial post— newly risen like a bull— well-placed and firmly fixed, anoints the victims.
Upon the strewn sacrificial grass, while the fire is kindled, the Adhvaryu priest has stood up, full of joy.
Like a herdsman, Agni, the Hotṛ-priest, goes three times around from of old, choosing his path.
Agni, the measured-strider, goes around by himself—the Hotṛ-priest, delightful, sweet-voiced, and true to the Law.
His flames run like prize-winning horses; all beings are afraid when he has blazed forth.

Auspicious is your appearance, O Agni, you of the fair countenance; beautiful is the sight of you, though you are terrible and manifold. For your radiance they do not obstruct with darkness, nor do the defilers bring any stain upon your body.
There is no one who has warded off his birth, nor indeed have mother and father been able to restrain him when he desires to go forth.
Then Agni, the purifier, well-established like Mitra, has shone among the human clans.
Him, Agni, whom the five sisters dwelling together have brought forth twice among the human tribes—
him who awakens at dawn, like a sharpened tooth, bright and fair-tongued, keen as an axe.
O Agni, those bay steeds of yours— bathed in ghee, ruddy, straight-moving, swift-moving, bright-red, virile, and with straight testicles— wondrous ones, have called upon the assembly of the gods.
Those flames of thine, O Agni, which move along, all-conquering, unwearied, and brilliant—
like hawks hastening toward their goal, they roar loudly like the host of Maruts.
The prayer has been fashioned for you, O kindled one; let the reciter proclaim the hymn; you bestow it upon the sacrificer.
Men have seated Agni as the Hotṛ-priest, the desiring ones paying homage to him, the praise of the living man.
This one has been established here as the first by the ordainers, the most excellent invoker, to be praised at the sacrifices—
he whom Apnavāna and the Bhṛgus caused to shine forth, the wonderful and pervasive one, for every tribe within the woods.
O Agni, when will the manifestation of your divinity appear in its proper sequence?
For mortals have indeed seized you, who are to be praised among the people.
Beholding him, the observer of cosmic order (*ṛtāvān*), the wise one, like the sky with its stars,
as the bringer of joy to all sacrifices in every house.
The Āyus have brought hither the swift messenger of Vivasvat, who moves toward all peoples— the banner of the Bhr̥gus, for every tribe.
They have established him as the Hotṛ priest in due order— the wise one, the delightful one with purifying luster, the most excellent sacrificer through his seven stations.
Him who is enveloped in the eternal mothers, dwelling in the forest,
who is wonderful, hidden in the cave, yet easy to find for one who seeks him anywhere— him [I praise].
When the gods rejoiced in the separation of the grain within that udder, in the abode of *ṛta*,
great Agni— honored with reverence and offered oblations— has ever been present for the sacrifice as the guardian of *ṛta*.
Knowing the duties of the sacrifice as a messenger, and being fully cognizant of both ends of heaven and earth,
you go forth as a messenger from of old, chosen and most wise, knowing the ascents to heaven.
Black is your path, O radiant one; your light shines before you, and your moving flame is the very first of wondrous forms.
When she who has not yet spoken conceives you as her embryo, even as soon as you are born, you become a messenger.
The vigor of him who was born this very moment is visible when the wind blows after his flame;
he turns his sharp tongue among the dry brushwood, and with his jaws, he rends even solid food.

When he has carried away the food swiftly with his swift [strength], the mighty Agni makes himself a swift messenger; consuming [the offerings], he follows the roar of the wind; like a swift horse, he is urged forward and incited for the prize.
I urge with my song your messenger, the all-knowing, the immortal bearer of oblations, the most excellent sacrificer.
For he knows the treasury of wealth, the great ascent to heaven;
may he bring the gods here to us.
That god knows how to bend the gods to his will for the sake of the one who lives by the *ṛta* in his home; he bestows even the most cherished treasures.
He is the Hotṛ; he, being wise, goes between as a messenger, knowing the ascent to heaven.
May we be those who have honored Agni with offerings of oblations—
those who nourish him and kindle him.
They have become renowned far and wide, having won wealth and heroic powers,
they who have offered worship to Agni.
May riches, much-desired, come to us day by day; may strengths rise up for us.
That inspired sage, through his power over the human tribes,
pierces through them like a swift arrow.
O Agni, be gracious; you are great, you who have come to this god-seeking people to sit upon the sacred grass.
Difficult to deceive among human clans, the immortal one has become a messenger for all, a protector.
He is led around the sacrificial seat as the joyous Hotṛ-priest during the rites of heaven; and he sits down also as the Potṛ-priest.
And Agni is the divine wife at the sacrifice; he is also the master of the house in the home; and he sits down as the Brahman priest.
For you come as the invoker of the people who perform the sacrifice,
and [you take] the oblations of human beings.
He indeed performs the office of messenger for him whose sacrifice you have enjoyed,
in order to carry the mortal's oblation.
O Aṅgiras, find pleasure in our ritual; [find pleasure] in our sacrifice;
hear our invocation.
May your unassailable chariot reach us from every side,
O Lord, with which you protect those who offer oblations.
O Agni, may we today further this [hymn] for you with our praises— as one would a horse— with auspicious resolve that touches the heart,
through our offerings.
For thus, O Agni, you have become the charioteer of auspicious will, of effective skill, and of the lofty cosmic order.
Through these our hymns, O Agni, come hither toward us like the light of heaven; be well-disposed toward us with all your faces.
Praising you today with these songs, O Agni, let us serve you; your roars thunder forth like those of heaven.
O Agni, your most sweet appearance shines forth even now at daybreak and even now at nightfall;
it glows for glory like a golden ornament close at hand.
Like purified ghee, like a stainless body, like bright gold— so does that [splendor] of yours shine, O self-dependent one, like a golden ornament.
For you, O Agni, observer of Truth, drive away even long-standing enmity from the mortal who thus sacrifices to you.
May our friendship with you gods, O Agni, be auspicious; may it be our kinship in this common dwelling, at this same udder.
Auspicious is your face, O powerful Agni; it shines forth near the sun. Bright to behold, it is seen even by night; in its form, food is visible, unblemished for the sight.
O Agni, born of many, being praised with fervor, open up the inspired thought for the singer through your power;
O radiant one of great majesty, grant us that abundant prayer which you have favored with all the gods.
From you, O Agni, are born poetic insights, from you inspired thoughts, and from you arise hymns that bring success;
from you comes wealth adorned with heroes for the mortal who offers oblations with a focused mind.
From you is born the prize-winning steed who brings booty, far-reaching, performing deeds of aid, and truly powerful;
from you comes wealth impelled by the gods, bringing bliss; and from you, O Agni, comes the swift, speeding charger.

O Agni, the mortals seeking the gods first invite you, the immortal god with the pleasant tongue; with their prayers they seek to win you, the one who drives away hatred, the domestic lord of the house, the unerring.

Far from us, O Agni, you drive away lack of insight, far away distress, and far away every evil thought, when you protect us. O Son of Strength, auspicious at evening, O God, he whom you accompany brings well-being.
O Agni, he who kindles you with the ladle uplifted, and prepares food for you three times on this very day—
may he excel through glorious splendors, prevailing by your wisdom, O Jātavedas, you who are full of insight.
O Agni, he who, laboring with great devotion, brings fuel to you while honoring your majesty—
he, kindling you at evening and at dawn, prospers and dwells with wealth, slaying his enemies.
Agni is the lord of great dominion; Agni is the master of booty and the highest wealth.
Most youthful and self-dependent, he bestows treasure upon the mortal who serves him according to his custom.
Whatever offense we have committed against you, O youngest one, among men, through lack of thought or by any other act, make us sinless before Aditi; loosen our transgressions on every side, O Agni.
O Agni, even from great transgression, in the presence of both gods and mortals, may we, your friends, never suffer harm; grant health and prosperity to our children and descendants.
Just as you, O Vasus, worthy of worship, released even the Gaurī cow that was stuck by the foot, so do you release us from this distress; O Agni, further prolong our life.
Agni has looked back upon the vanguard of the dawns as they shine forth, well-disposed toward the bestowing of treasures.
O Aśvins, come to the dwelling of the righteous man; the god Sūrya rises up with his light.
The god Savitṛ has sent his light upward, shaking off the drop like a warrior seeking cattle;
Varuṇa and Mitra follow their decree when they cause Sūrya to ascend to heaven.
Him whom they made for the dispersal of darkness, while remaining steadfast in their dwellings and seeking no other goal—
him, Sūrya, the all-seeing, the seven mighty bay mares carry through the entire moving world.
Moving with your swiftest steeds, you go weaving the thread, O God, spreading out the black garment. The rays of the Sun, quivering, have driven away the darkness within the waters like a skin.
Unsupported and unbound, how is it that this one does not fall down, face downward or face upward?
By what inherent power does he move? Who has seen him? As the pillar of heaven, he stands joined together and protects the firmament.
Agni Jātavedas, the god, has looked upon the Dawns as they shine with their splendors. O Nāsatyas, you of wide stride, come hither to this our sacrifice on your chariot.
The god Savitṛ has raised his banner aloft, creating light for the entire world;
Sūrya, shining brightly with his rays, has filled heaven, earth, and the mid-air.
Bringing light, the ruddy ones have come; great and wonderful, she shines brightly with her rays.
Awakening us for our welfare, the goddess Dawn approaches on her well-yoked chariot.
May those most excellent carriers bring you both here—chariots and horses—at the dawning of the dawn.
For these Soma juices are for your drinking of the honey; O Bulls, rejoice at this sacrifice!
Unsupported and unattached, how is it that this one does not fall down, face downward or face upward?
By what inherent power does he move? Who has seen him? As the pillar of heaven, he stands firm and protects the firmament.
Agni, our Hotṛ at the sacrifice, being a prize-winning steed, is led around—
the god worthy of worship among the gods.
Agni goes three times around the sacrifice like a charioteer,
bestowing nourishment upon the gods.
Agni, the sage and lord of booty, has stepped around the oblations,
bestowing treasures upon the donor.
This [Agni], who is kindled for Sṛñjaya, the son of Devavāta—
resplendent and the subduer of enemies— is present here.
May a mortal man indeed be the master of this Agni, who is so heroic, sharp-toothed, and bountiful.
Him they groom day after day, like a prize-winning steed, like the ruddy child of heaven.
When the prince Sāhadevya awakened me with his two bay horses,
I rose up toward him like one summoned.
And those two adorable bay horses, presented by the prince Sāhadevya,
I accepted immediately.
O divine Aśvins, may this son of Sahadeva, Somaka Kumāra, live a long life for you both.
O divine Aśvins, you two make that prince Sāhadevya long-lived.
May the true Maghavan, the drinker of the dregs, come hither; may his bay steeds run toward us.
For him we have pressed the most skillful soma-juice; being praised here, may he grant us his presence.
O Hero, descend like [a traveler] at the end of his journey, so that you may rejoice today at this our libation.
Like Uśanas, the wise priest shall recite a hymn; let him offer a prayer to the conscious Asura.
Like a sage accomplishing secret insights, when the bull, drinking deeply, shall sing his outpouring;
thus from heaven he brought forth the seven singers, who by day performed their works while chanting.
When the beautiful light of heaven was found through hymns, they made the great radiance shine at the break of day;
the most heroic one, in his desire to help, has dispelled the blinding and turbid darkness so that men may see.
Indra, the consumer of the *ṛjīṣa*, has grown to immeasurable power; with his greatness he has filled both worlds, heaven and earth.
Even beyond that, his majesty extends further, for he has surpassed all existing beings.
Śakra, knowing all manly deeds, released the waters with his eager friends;
they who by their words even split the rock, the *uśij* opened the stall full of cattle.
You struck down Vṛtra who had obstructed the waters; the earth, being conscious, favored your thunderbolt. You sent forth the oceanic floods; O bold hero, you became their lord through your might.
When you, O much-invoked one, shattered the rock and brought forth the waters, Saramā appeared before you;
as our leader, praised by the Aṅgirases, may you burst open the cow-pens and win for us abundant booty.

O Maghavan, you who are mindful of men, come toward the sage for our aid in the winning of light for him who implores you; speed him with your protections at the invocation for glory. Let the guileful Dasyu, devoid of prayer, be brought low.
Come home with a mind intent on slaying the Dasyus; let Kutsa be devoted to your friendship.
Sit down together in your own dwelling, you two of like form; for the woman who knows the Truth indeed discerns between you two.
You go on the same chariot with Kutsa, seeking aid, as the driver of Vāta’s two bay steeds, you who are their lord;
desiring to win the prize like a straight-running horse, the Seer shall be present for the decisive day.
For Kutsa, you struck down the insatiable Śuṣṇa; at the onset of the day, you crushed Kuyava and thousands of Dasyus.
Immediately, with the aid of Kutsa, crush the Dasyus and strike off the wheel of Sūrya in the encounter.
You delivered Pipru Mṛgayu, who had grown exceedingly strong, into the power of R̥jiśvan, the son of Vidathin;
you struck down fifty thousand black ones and shattered his fortresses as if they were an earthen vessel.
When the Sun, placing his body near [the earth], manifests your form, O immortal one—
like a wild elephant putting on its strength, like a terrifying lion bearing his weapons.
Desiring wealth, our wishes have gone toward Indra, longing for him at the pressing of the juice as if for the winning of light;
seeking glory and striving with hymns, he is like a home, like a joyous and fair-to-see abundance.
Let us invoke that very Indra, who is easy to call upon, he who has performed many heroic deeds;
he who, possessing desirable wealth, swiftly brings booty fit for a singer like me to be seized.
When the sharp bolt falls among the people, O Hero, upon whichever one it may fall in their moment of confusion;
when the terrible encounter with the noble foe occurs—then indeed, be the protector of our bodies.
Be the protector of Vāmadeva’s inspired thoughts; be his friend, free from malice, in the winning of booty.
We have come to you for your providence; O you of wide renown, be ever present for the singer.
With these men who seek you, O Indra, with these liberal patrons, O Maghavan, in every battle—
surpassing our enemies with splendors like the heavens— we would rejoice through many nights and autumns.

Thus have we fashioned this prayer for Indra, the bull, the strong one, just as the Bhṛgus fashioned a chariot. May our friendship never be severed; may he be our fierce protector and guardian of our bodies.

Now, O Indra, being praised and glorified, cause nourishment to swell for the singer like rivers; a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of Bay Steeds. Through our devotion, may we be chariot-borne victors, ever victorious.
Great art thou, O Indra; indeed, the earth and the heaven have recognized thy dominion with great magnificence.
Having slain Vṛtra with thy might, thou didst release the rivers that had been swallowed by the serpent.
At the birth of your brilliance, the sky trembled; the earth trembled from fear of your own wrath.
The firm mountains roared; the wastes were dissolved and the waters flowed away.

Splitting the mountain with his might, hurling the thunderbolt while manifesting his conquering power, he, the exhilarated one, slew Vṛtra with his bolt; the waters, their strength now struck down, flowed forth with speed.

Your father, the Sky, deemed himself a true hero; the maker of Indra performed the most skillful work—he who begat him, the one with the resonant voice and the excellent thunderbolt, as immovable as the earth from its seat.
He who alone causes the earth to tremble, the king of the peoples, Indra invoked by many—
truly all rejoice in him, praising the gift of this divine and bounteous lord.
All Soma juices have become his; all the most intoxicating draughts of the mighty one have indeed become his.
You have truly become the lord of treasures; O Indra, you have placed all the peoples within your gift.
Then, O Indra, as soon as you were first born, you established all these peoples;
O Maghavan, with your thunderbolt you rent asunder the dragon who lay across the flowing waters.
Indra, the ever-conquering, the bold, the powerful, the great, the boundless bull with the excellent thunderbolt—
he who is the slayer of Vṛtra, the winner of booty, and the giver of riches, the bountiful Maghavan.
This one, chosen and renowned alone as Maghavan in battles, drives away the assembled hosts.
He brings the prize of victory which he wins; may we be dear to him in his friendship.
This one is heard of as conquering and slaying; he also wins the cattle by battle.
When Indra makes his wrath true, everything firm and everything moving fears him.

Indra has won the cattle, he has won the gold, and he, the bounteous Maghavan, has won the herds of horses—he who [conquered] many [enemies]. With these men, the most heroic one, by his powers, he is the distributor of wealth and the gatherer of riches.
How much does Indra surpass his mother, how much his father, the progenitor who begot him?
He who, like the wind driven by impetuous thundering clouds, stirs up his own vigor in an instant.
He makes the settled man unsettled; Maghavan raises up the dust in a whirlwind.
Like the sky armed with lightning, he shatters all; and Maghavan bestows wealth upon his praiser.
This one has impelled the wheel of the sun; he has brought Etaśa to rest as he was speeding along.
The black, winding smoke besprinkles him at the base of the skin, in the womb of this region.
Like a sacrificing priest at the black [sacrificial post].

Desiring cattle for friendship, O sages, desiring horses, desiring strength, and desiring wives, we urge Indra— the bull who bestows offspring and possesses inexhaustible aid— downward like a water-jar from a well.

Be our protector, appearing as a kinsman; be the overseer and the comforter of those who offer Soma. As a friend, a father, and the most fatherly of fathers, create a world for the one who desires it, bestowing vital strength.
Be the protector of those who seek your friendship; as our friend, O Indra, being praised, bestow vital strength upon the one who lauds you.
For we have exerted ourselves for you with these ritual labors, magnifying you, O Indra.
When Indra Maghavan is praised, he alone slays many Vṛtras that are irresistible;
dear is the singer to him, under whose protection neither gods nor mortals can obstruct him.
Thus may Indra, the bounteous, the overflowing, the unassailable upholder of the people, make our prayers true;
you, by your very birth, are the king—bestow upon us, for the singer, great renown.

Now, O Indra, being praised and now being lauded, swell nourishment for the singer like rivers; a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of Bay Steeds. Through our devotion, may we be charioteers who ever win the prize.
This is the path discovered of old, by which all the gods were born; from this very place let him, having grown strong, be born anew. Let him not cause his mother to perish in that way.
I have not emerged from this; it is a difficult path. I shall go out sideways, across the flanks.
Much remains for me to do that has not yet been done. I will fight with this one and question that one.
He looked after his departing mother: "I shall not go back; indeed, I shall now go forth. In the house of Tvaṣṭṛ, Indra drank the Soma, a hundredfold portion of the juice pressed in the ladles.
What could he accomplish separately, whom she bore for a thousand months and many autumns?
Indeed, there is no likeness of him among those already born nor among those yet to be born.
Considering him as if something blameworthy, the Mother hid Indra, who was overflowing with heroic power;
then he rose up, clothing himself in his own raiment, and as he was being born, he filled the two worlds, heaven and earth.
These flow along, sounding *alala*, crying out like the followers of Truth (*ṛtāvarī*);
ask them: what is this they are saying? Against what rock-bound enclosure do the waters break through?
What indeed do the waters proclaim as the secret invocations for him; do they intend to reveal the hidden power of Indra?
Having struck down Vṛtra with his mighty weapon, my son has released these rivers.
Even me, the young woman, did not abandon you; even me, Kuṣavā swallowed you.
Even for my sake, the waters were gracious to the infant; even for my sake, Indra rose up with might.
Even my own shoulder-joint, O Maghavan, you struck down after having pierced it;
then, having been pierced, he became inferior, as you crushed the head of the Dāsa with your weapon.
The first-calf cow has brought forth for you the ancient, invincible, and impetuous bull, Indra.
The mother has let loose the unlicked calf to wander, he who seeks a path for his own body by himself.
And the Mother looked with favor upon the Great Bull; "O son, these gods are abandoning you," she said.
Then Indra, about to slay Vṛtra, spoke: "O friend Viṣṇu, stride out yet more widely!"
Who made your mother a widow? Who sought to kill you as you were wandering? Which god was there to show you mercy when you seized your father by the foot and slew him?
Helplessly, I cooked the entrails of a dog; among the gods I found no one to comfort me. I saw my wife being dishonored, and then the falcon brought the honeyed nectar to me.
Thus, O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, all the gods, the swift-invokers, your helpers, choose you alone—
the great, the exalted, the grown one— as the sole one for the slaying of Vṛtra, even as both the worlds choose him.
The gods released [the waters] like those who have grown old; O Indra, you became the sovereign ruler whose womb is truth.
You slew the serpent who lay encompassing the flood; you dug out the channels that nourish all things.
O Indra, with your thunderbolt you rent asunder at a non-joint the dragon who was not yet satisfied, who was spread out, who was unawakened, who was sleeping,
and who lay across the seven downward-flowing rivers.
Indra shook the earth with his might, as the wind shakes the water with its powers;
he burst apart even the firm things, exerting his strength, and struck down the peaks of the mountains.
They have run forth toward him like women toward their embryo; the pressing-stones have gone forth together like chariots.
You have satisfied the far-spreading rivers, you have pressed down the waves; O Indra, you have released the obstructed floods.
You [O Indra] brought to rest the great river, flowing with all-sustaining milk for Turvīti and Vayya;
you checked the surging flood through homage and made the rivers easy to cross, O Indra.
Like roaring rivers from the springs, he made the youthful, flowing waters swell;
he filled the thirsty deserts and plains. Indra brought down the barren cows, the wives of the wondrous one.
Through many dawns and many celebrated autumns, having slain Vṛtra, he released the rivers;
Indra pierced the obstructed, closely confined streams so that they might flow across the earth.
O Lord of the Bay Horses, you brought forth from his dwelling the son of the unwedded woman, whom the ants had not given;
the blind man saw clearly as he grasped the serpent, and the jar-breaker emerged, his joints coming together.
The inspired sage, knowing them, has proclaimed your ancient deeds to the wise one—
those acts which you, O King, have performed according to your own will as manly and virile exploits.

Now, O Indra, being praised and glorified, swell nourishment for the singer like rivers; a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of Bay Steeds. Through our devotion, may we be charioteers who ever win the prize.

May Indra, the fierce lord of men, the wielder of the thunderbolt in his arm, come to our aid from afar or from near at hand, performing protection for us; may he, victorious in the clash of battles, overcome those who attack us with his mightiest powers.
May Indra come toward us with his bay horses, turning hitherward for our protection and for bounty.
May the wielder of the thunderbolt, the bounteous and exuberant one, stand by this sacrifice of ours in the struggle for booty.
O Indra, placing this sacrifice of ours before you, you shall grant us our purpose;
like a gambler winning wealth, O wielder of the thunderbolt, may we conquer the enemy in battle through you.

Desiring us and well-disposed, O self-dependent Indra, come indeed toward us from nearby; drink now of this well-pressed Soma, of the offered honey-sweet draught, and exhilarate yourself with the soma-juice that flows along the back.
Him who has overflowed with abundance through the new seers, like a ripe tree, like a victorious sickle—
like a youth longing for a maiden, I call toward me Indra, the one invoked by many.
Like a mountain, Indra is self-strong and lofty; from of old he was born fierce for the sake of conquest.
Like a formidable and ancient wielder of the thunderbolt, he has shattered [the clouds]; like a vessel filled with water, he is overflowing with wealth.
He whose peer there has never been since birth, nor anyone who can obstruct his bounty or his great wealth—
showering forth like fierce power, O you who are invoked by many, grant us riches.
I behold the wealth and the dwelling of the people; you shall open the stall of the cattle. O helper of men, victorious in battles, you lead us toward a vast heap of riches.

By what power is he heard as the most powerful, by which the lofty one repeatedly performs his various deeds? He who is best at dispersing the distress of the liberal donor, then bestows wealth upon the singer.
Do not neglect us; bring it, give that to us—abundant wealth which you have to bestow upon the donor.
When this new gift is praised and this hymn is recited, we shall proclaim it, O Indra, while offering our praise.
Now, O Indra, being praised and now being lauded, cause nourishment to swell for the singer like rivers;
a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of the Bay Steeds. Through our devotion, may we be masters of chariots and eternal victors.
May Indra come to us for our protection; here, being praised, may the hero be our companion at the feast.
May he, whose many powers have increased, nourish his sovereign dominion like the sky, so that it may prevail over all.
Here, celebrate his manly powers—he of many glories and abundant wealth—among men;
he whose will is like a sovereign in the assembly, who, as a victorious overcomer, prevails over the peoples.
May Indra come from heaven, from earth, swiftly from the ocean or from the watery expanse;
may he come with the Maruts for our protection, either from the realm of light or from the distant seat of Cosmic Order.
We shall praise Indra in the assemblies— that great lord who rules over massive wealth,
who with Vāyu conquers in the cattle-rich lands, and who boldly leads us toward better fortune.
He who, establishing himself in reverence upon reverence, raises his voice, generating it for the sake of sacrifice;
may that Hotṛ-priest, striving with hymns and possessing many boons, bring Indra here to the sacrificial seats.
When, through inspired thought, those seeking inspiration hasten to the pressing-stone in the dwelling of Auśija,
then may he come— the invincible Hotṛ of Pastyas, our great bearer of oblations within the secret enclosures.
When the strength of the bull Bhārvara truly accompanies him for the sake of the singer’s gift;
when he is in the secret lair of Auśija, as he goes forth for the sake of inspired thought, for refreshment, and for exhilaration.
When he opens wide the expanses of the mountain, he quickens the speed of the waters with his milks;
when the wise ones bring him forth for the sake of vigor, he finds the dwelling place of the bull and the wild ox.
Auspicious are your hands and well-fashioned your palms, O Indra, which bestow wealth upon the one who praises you.
What is your dwelling? Why do you not exhilarate us? Why do you not rise up to rejoice in giving?

Thus indeed is Indra the true sovereign of wealth; he slays Vṛtra and creates wide space for the people. Much-praised one, grant us riches through your wisdom; may I partake of your divine protection.

Now, O Indra, being praised and extolled, cause nourishment to swell for the singer like rivers; a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of Bay Steeds. Through our devotion, may we ever be chariot-borne victors.
Whatever Indra has enjoyed and whatever he desires, that shall the great and mighty one accomplish for us.
Maghavan, who goes wielding a stone by his strength, accepts our prayer, our hymn of praise, the Soma, and our recitations.
The bull, hurling his four-cornered thunderbolt, the fierce, most heroic, and powerful one with his two arms,
has clothed himself in wool for glory, seeking the Paruṣṇī river whose joints he has embraced for friendship.
The god who, being born as the most divine, [endowed] with great spoils and mighty strengths,
holding the eager thunderbolt in his arms, made the heaven tremble by his impetus and shook the earth.
All the embankments and the many slopes, the sky, and the earth trembled at his lofty birth;
the two parents bring forth the impetuous one like a bull, and the winds roar around him like men.
These indeed, O Indra, are your great deeds against the mighty, to be proclaimed at all the soma-pressings—
when you, O hero, bold one, having boldly displayed your courage, struck the dragon with your thunderbolt through your power.
O you of many heroic deeds, all those true [gifts] of yours stream forth from the udder of the bull;
then, indeed, O one with virile power, the rivers, fearing you, have rushed forward with speed.
Here, O Lord of the Bay Steeds, those divine sisters praised you with their aids, O Indra,
when you released them who were held fast, so that they might flow along your long-reaching path.
The exhilarating stalk has been pressed like a river; may the ritual effort and the power of the one who exerts himself come toward us.
Like the twin reins of a glowing steed, may the swift ray of the bull, possessed of mighty strength, draw you hither.
Bestow upon us the highest and most excellent manly powers, O ever-conquering one; grant us all victorious strengths.
Make the Vṛtras easy for us to slay; strike down the weapon of the attacking mortal.
O Indra, listen well to us alone; bestow wonderful spoils of war upon us.
Send all abundant blessings to us; O Maghavan, be truly a giver of cattle to us.

Now, O Indra, being praised and glorified, cause nourishment to swell for the singer like rivers; a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of the Bay Steeds. Through our devotion, may we ever be masters of chariots and victorious.
How has he grown great? Whose priest’s sacrifice does he favor as he approaches the Soma from the udder?
Drinking, desiring, and enjoying the plant, the lofty one has grown for the sake of wealth for the one who shines.

What hero has attained his common feast? Who has shared in his favors? What of him is wondrous? What has been perceived through his aid? How may he become the strengthener of the one who exerts himself in worship?
How does Indra hear the oblation being offered? How, hearing it, does he know of this [sacrificer’s] aids? What are his ancient manifestations? And how do they call him the fulfiller for the singer?
How may the one who exerts himself with devotion, meditating upon it, attain his wealth through this [hymn]?
May the god, the knower of all things, being pleased by our homage, accept that which is offered according to the cosmic order.

How, and at whose dawning of this dawn, has the god taken pleasure in the friendship of a mortal? How, and in what way, does he grant his friendship to those friends who have extended to him a well-yoked desire?
What indeed is this measureless friendship for our friends? When shall we proclaim your brotherhood?
For the sake of glory, the forms of him who is fair to behold are like the most wondrous light of heaven—the streams of nourishment from the cow.

Seeking to strike down the malicious and destructive one who is devoid of Indra, he sharpens his keen edges for the assault; where, like a fierce creditor collecting debts, the Mighty One has driven the unknown ones far away from the Dawns.
For the boons of *ṛta* are many; the thought of *ṛta* destroys crookedness.
The cry of *ṛta* has pierced the deaf ears of the living man, awakening him as he glows with fervor.
The firm foundations of *ṛta* exist; manifold are its bright and wondrous forms for the sake of beauty.
By means of *ṛta* they impel long-lasting nourishment; by means of *ṛta* the cows have entered into *ṛta*.
Upholding the *ṛta*, he wins the very *ṛta*; the force of the *ṛta* is swift and seeks cattle.
For the sake of the *ṛta*, the broad, vast, and deep earth exists; for the sake of the *ṛta*, the two supreme milch-cows yield their milk.

Now, O Indra, being praised and glorified, cause nourishment to swell for the singer like rivers; a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of the Bay Steeds. Through our devotion, may we be charioteers who ever win the prize.
What excellent praise will turn Indra, the son of strength, toward us with his bounty?
For that hero, O people, bestows riches upon the singer; he is the lord of cattle who drives away our adversaries.
He is to be invoked and praised in the slaying of Vṛtra; that Indra is well-praised and true to his bounty.
On his journey, may the bountiful Maghavan grant wide space to the mortal who offers prayers and presses the Soma.

Him indeed the men invoke in the encounter; risking their bodies, they make him their protector, when both sides, the men, have come together to one another’s sacrifice for the winning of offspring and progeny.

The people strive for power in their exertion; the fierce ones, panting together in the contest for waters, when the warrior tribes have come together, then some indeed act like Indra in the encounter.
Then indeed some shall worship the power of Indra; then let the cooked offering surpass the sacrificial cake;
then let Soma overwhelm those who do not press it; then indeed he has taken pleasure to sacrifice to the Bull.
He who presses the Soma for Indra who desires it thus, he creates wide space for himself;
with a focused mind, not turning away, he makes that very person his friend in battles.
Whoever shall press Soma for Indra today, shall cook the cooked offerings, and shall roast the grains— Indra,
delighting in that man's hymns, shall bestow upon him virile strength.
When the impetuous one has discerned the battle, when the noble one has looked toward the long contest,
the wife calls out to the bull, sharpened by the Soma-pressers, toward the dwelling.
He traded a greater price for a lesser one; having sold it, I regretted it when I went back.
He did not overreach by taking more for less; those with skill and wit milk out the profit.
"Who will buy this Indra of mine for ten milch-cows? When he has struck down the Vṛtras, then let him give him back to me."

Now, O Indra, being praised and lauded, cause nourishment to swell for the singer like rivers; a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of Bay Steeds. Through our devotion, may we be chariot-borne victors, ever victorious.
Who today, a manly lover of the gods, desiring it, has taken pleasure in the friendship of Indra? Or who, when the fire is kindled and the Soma is pressed, prays for great, decisive aid?
Who has bowed with speech to the one worthy of Soma? Who becomes mindful as the dawns break?
Who desires Indra’s alliance, who his friendship, and who his brotherhood? And who, for the sake of the sage, desires his protection?
Who today chooses the protection of the gods? Who prays to the Ādityas and Aditi for light?
Whose pressed stalk of soma do the Aśvins, Indra, and Agni drink with their minds, finding it agreeable?
To him may Agni Bhārata grant protection; may he long behold the rising sun—he who says, "Let us press the Soma for Indra," for the hero, the manly, the most heroic among men.
Neither many nor few overcome him; Aditi shall grant him wide protection.
Dear to the well-doer, dear to Indra is the thoughtful one; dear is the helpful one, dear is his Soma-drinker.
This hero, the swift-conquering Indra, is easy to serve; he makes the cooked offering his own exclusive property.
He is neither a kinsman, nor a friend, nor a relative to one who does not press the Soma; he is difficult to serve for the one who offers no libations and speaks no words of praise.
Indra, the drinker of the pressed juice, does not form a friendship with the wealthy miser who does not press the soma.
He seizes his wealth and strikes him bare; he becomes the exclusive protector for the one who presses the juice and cooks the offering.
The higher ones, the lower, and those in the middle—those going forth and those resting—call upon Indra;
those dwelling in peace and those fighting, men seeking booty, call upon Indra.
I was Manu and I was Sūrya; I am the seer Kakṣīvat, the inspired singer. I have guided Kutsa, the son of Arjuni; I am the sage Uśanas—behold me!
I gave the earth to the noble one; I gave rain to the mortal who offers oblations.
I led forth the lowing waters; the gods followed my will.
Intoxicated, I shattered the ninety-nine fortresses of Śambara all at once; with you as my ally, I utterly destroyed the hundredth stronghold when I protected Divodāsa Atithigva.
Let that hero be superior to the Maruts, and let the falcon, swift-flying,
be superior to the other falcons, when he, the fair-winged one, by his own inherent power and without wheels, brought the god-pleasing oblation to Manu.
When the bird, trembling, brought [the gift] from there, the path was released, wide and ruddy, swift as thought;
it went quickly with the honeyed Soma, and thus the falcon won glory here.

The straight-flying falcon, the bird, bringing the exhilarating intoxication from afar, has brought the Soma while grasping the stalk; he, the friend of the gods, having taken it from yonder highest heaven.
Taking it, the falcon brought the Soma—ten thousand and a hundred thousand libations at once.
There, the wise one abandoned his enemies in the exhilaration of Soma; the undeluded one [left behind] the deluded.
While still in the womb, I indeed knew all the generations of these gods. A hundred iron fortresses guarded me; then, like a hawk, I flew out with speed.
Indeed, he did not carry me off against my will; through his skill and heroic power, he overcame him.
Purandhi abandoned her hostilities, and he, swelling with strength, crossed over the winds.
When the falcon swooped down from heaven, or when the winds bore Purandhi away;
when Kṛśānu, the archer, eager in his mind, released the swift-drawing bowstring for him.
Like Bhujyu, the swift-flying falcon bore him from the high ridge, he who possesses Indra. His winged feather fell within; this was the mark of the bird as it sped on its course.
Then Maghavan has taken for his exhilaration the white jar, anointed with milk, swelling with the bright juice;
the first of the honey, offered by the *adhvaryu*s, Indra, the hero, has accepted it to drink for his exhilaration—he has accepted it to drink for his exhilaration.

With you as his ally, O Soma, through that friendship of yours, Indra caused the waters to flow for mankind. He slew the serpent, released the seven rivers, and opened the channels that had been closed up.
With you as his ally, O Indu, Indra by his might suddenly struck down the wheel of Sūrya, which was rolling upon the high ridge; thus was all the life-force of the great oppressor destroyed.
Indra slew them and Agni consumed them, O Indu; before midday, in the encounter, he struck down the Dasyus.
With his arrow, he felled many thousands, as if by design, upon those who were fleeing in difficult terrain and wretched dwellings.
O Indra, you made the Dasyus lower than all; you made the Dāsa tribes infamous.
You two drove them back and crushed the enemies; you obtained recompense through your weapons of slaughter.
Thus it is true, O bounteous ones: you two, Indra and Soma, have disclosed the stall of horses and cattle;
you have burst open the enclosures that were barred by stone and have overflowed even the earths as they broke through.
Come to us, O Indra, being praised, with your strengths and aids, exhilarated by the *haris* steeds;
passing even over the many libations of the enemy, you who are celebrated with hymns as one whose bounty is true.
For he, the manly one who perceives, comes indeed when invoked by the pressers to the sacrifice—
he who, possessing good horses and being fearless in his own estimation, rejoices with the Soma-pressers and with heroes.
May he cause his ears to hear so that he may seek booty; may he gladden him according to the beloved direction.
Raining down for the sake of bounty, the mighty Indra shall make for us good paths and security.
He who comes with his aid to the one imploring him, to the inspired singer who thus calls upon him and praises him—
placing swift steeds upon the yoke-pole by his own power, he whose arm wields the thunderbolt brings thousands and hundreds.

O Maghavan Indra, may we, the inspired singers, be protected by you; may we be patrons who praise you, having obtained a share of the wealth from the lofty heaven—wealth that is desirable and rich in nourishment—for its bestowal.
O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, there is none superior to you, nor any greater than you;
indeed, there is no one else like you.
All the peoples have indeed followed you, as wheels turn after a chariot;
truly, you are renowned as great.
Even all the gods together could not withstand you, O Indra,
when you extended the days by night.
And where, for the sake of those who were oppressed, O Indra, you stole the sun from Kutsa as he was fighting.
Where you alone, O Indra, fought against all the impetuous gods, you struck down the attackers.
And where, O Indra, you set free the sun for the sake of the mortal,
you protected Etaśa with your powers.
Why indeed, O Vṛtra-slayer, are you so exceedingly wrathful, O Maghavan? It was then that you struck down Dānu.
And this indeed was the heroic deed, O Indra, the manly exploit you performed:
that you slew the daughter of Heaven, she who was ill-disposed toward marriage.
Even the daughter of heaven, the great one who was exalting herself—
O Indra, you crushed Uṣas.
Uṣas ran away from the chariot, terrified by the crushed [chariot],
when the bull struck her down.
This wagon of hers lies here, utterly crushed by the Vipāś;
he has sped away to the far distance.
And by thy power, O Indra, thou didst encompass with thy magic might the Sindhu, which had spread itself wide over the earth.
And with bold courage, you stripped away the wealth of Śuṣṇa when you crushed his fortresses.
And you struck down Śambara, the Dāsa son of Kulitara, from the lofty mountain, O Indra.
And you slew the hundreds of thousands of the Dāsa Varcin,
as if [stripping] five fellies from a wheel.
And furthermore, Indra, the Lord of a hundred powers, caused that son of the unwedded woman who had been cast away to take his share in the hymns of praise.
Moreover, Indra, the Lord of Might, knowing well, brought across those two, Turvaśa and Yadu, who were unable to swim.
And those two Āryas, O Indra, you slew on the far side of the Sarayu;
you struck down Arṇa and Citraratha.
O slayer of Vṛtra, you have led away two who were abandoned—the blind and the lame.
That favor of yours is not to be attained [by others].
Indra shattered a hundred fortresses made of stone for Divodāsa, who offered him oblations.
With his weapons, Indra, through his power of illusion, put thirty thousand Dāsas to sleep for the sake of Dabhīti.
And you indeed, O Vṛtra-slayer Indra, are the common lord of cattle,
you who have shaken all these things.
And now, O Indra, whatever manly deed you shall perform with your power—
may no one today diminish that.
O Āduri, may the god Aryaman grant you what is desirable;
may Pūṣan grant what is desirable, Bhaga grant what is desirable, and the god Karūlatī grant what is desirable.
With what aid will the wondrous one come to us, he who is the ever-increasing friend? With what most powerful company?
Which true one among the exhilarations, most generous, shall intoxicate you with the soma-juice?
[He who] breaks open even the firmest wealth.
May you, the protector of us, your friends and singers, come toward us; may you be with a hundred aids.
Turn toward us like the rolling wheel of a steed, with the teams of horses belonging to the people.
For you come down the slope of our intentions as if to your own station; I have partaken [of the light] together with Sūrya.
When thy many wrathful impulses and thy wheels, O Indra, have sped forth together,
then [they are] in thee and in the sun.
Moreover, they indeed call you Maghavan, O Lord of Might,
the giver who does not hesitate.
And indeed, at once to the one who has labored and presses the juice,
you bestow abundant wealth.
For not even a hundred obstructors can restrain your bounty, nor can they hinder the mighty deeds you are about to perform.
May your hundred aids protect us; may your thousand aids protect us;
may all your succors protect us.
Choose us here for friendship and for well-being,
for great and heavenly wealth.
Favor us always, O Indra, with abundant wealth;
favor us with all your protections.
For us, open up those water-filled enclosures rich in cattle, like a hunter, O Indra, with your newest aids.
Our chariot, bold, radiant, and unshakable by Indra,
goes forth seeking cattle and horses.
O Sūrya, among the gods, establish for us a preeminent glory,
most lofty like the sky above.
Come then to our side, O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra; come with your great and mighty aids.
O Wondrous One, you are indeed swift and impetuous among those who possess wondrous powers;
you perform wonders for our protection.
Even with a few, you slay the more numerous and the mighty with your power—
those who are your companions.
O Indra, we are with you; we sing our praise to you. Protect us, indeed, each and every one of us!
O wielder of the stone, come to us with your wondrous, blameless, and unassailable aids.
O Indra, may we truly become the friends of one such as you, who possesses cattle, joined with you for the sake of impetuous strength.
For you alone, O Indra, rule over wealth consisting of cattle; as such, grant us abundant nourishment.
They cannot turn you away from another course when, being praised, O Indra, lover of songs, you wish to bestow wealth upon those who laud you.
The Gotamas have sung toward you with their song, O Indra, so that you may grant your gifts for the sake of spirited strength.
We shall proclaim your heroic deeds, those which you, rejoicing, shattered by attacking the fortresses of the Dāsas.
The wise ones sing those manly deeds which you have performed for them,
O Indra, lover of songs, when the juices are pressed.
The Gotamas have increased their strength through you, O Indra, bringing hymns of praise;
bestow upon them glory accompanied by heroic sons.
For even though you, O Indra, belong in common to all people who exist in succession,
we invoke you as such.
O Vasu, be turned toward us; O Indra, drinker of Soma, exhilarate yourself well with our soma-juices.
May the hymn of our thoughts bring you hither, O Indra;
turn your two bay steeds toward us.
Eat our sacrificial cake and take pleasure in our songs,
as one desiring a bride [delights] in a young woman.
We implore Indra for a thousand harnessed steeds;
a hundred jars of Soma.
We cause hundreds and thousands of your cattle to flow toward us;
may your bounty come to us.
Ten golden jars of yours we have received;
you are a great giver, O slayer of Vṛtra.
O bounteous giver, give us much; let not little come to us, but bring much hither.
For indeed, O Indra, you desire to bestow abundance.
For you are renowned in many places as a bountiful giver, O hero, slayer of Vṛtra;
grant us a share in your wealth.
O far-seeing one, grandson of the winner of cattle, I praise your two tawny steeds; do not hold back the cows from them.
Like two young girls, uncovered on a new wooden seat,
the two brown ones shine forth during their journeys.
Ready for me is the one who comes at dawn, ready is he who follows after dawn; the two tawny ones are unfailing on their journeys.
I send forth my speech like a messenger to the Ṛbhus; I pray for the white cow Śvaitarī as a sacrificial covering.
They who, impelled by the wind, with their swift movements, have in an instant become active all around the sky.

When the Ṛbhus performed service for their parents with their skillful deeds and wondrous powers, then indeed they attained the friendship of the gods; as wise ones, they brought nourishment to the mind.
May those who made their parents young again, who were lying old like worn-out sacrificial posts—
Vāja, Vibhvan, and Ṛbhu, accompanied by Indra and possessing the essence of sweetness— protect our sacrifice.
Since for a year the Ṛbhus guarded the cow, since for a year the Ṛbhus fashioned the skin,
and since for a year they carried her light— by these labors they attained immortality.
The eldest said, "Let us make two cups"; the younger said, "Let us make three";
the youngest said, "Let us make four. Tvaṣṭṛ was amazed at these words of yours, O Ṛbhus.
The men spoke the truth, for they indeed accomplished this; the Ṛbhus followed this self-dependent path.
Tvaṣṭṛ, having seen them, was amazed at the four brilliantly shining cups as if at the gods themselves.
When for twelve days the Ṛbhus rejoiced in the hospitality of Agohya while sleeping,
they made the fields fertile, led forth the rivers, established plants upon the desert, and brought the waters to the lowlands.

May those R̥bhus— who fashioned the well-rolling chariot that carries men, and who created the cow that quickens all and possesses every form— fashion wealth for us, they who are self-strong, skillful in their work, and dexterous of hand.
For the gods took pleasure in their waters, contemplating them with wisdom and mind;
Vāja became the skillful worker among the gods, Ṛbhukṣan that of Indra, and Vibhvan that of Varuṇa.
O Ṛbhus, those who, rejoicing with wisdom and hymns, fashioned for Indra the two well-yoked bay horses—
bestow upon us an increase of wealth and riches, O Ṛbhus, acting like friends who desire our welfare.
Today they have granted you the drinking of the soma and intoxication; O gods, it is not without toil that one gains friendship. Therefore, O Ṛbhus, bestow riches upon us now at this third libation.
O Ṛbhu, Vibhvan, Vāja, and Indra, come to this sacrifice of ours for the bestowing of treasures;
for now the goddess Dhiṣaṇā has assigned the drinking of you gods at these days, and your exhilarations have come together.
Knowing your origin, O Ṛbhus, you who possess the treasure of strength, rejoice according to the seasons!
Your exhilarations have come together, as has your abundance; send forth wealth consisting of brave heroes upon us.
O Ṛbhus, this sacrifice has been prepared for you, which you have accepted as you did from Manu of old.
You have come toward it with delight; O Vājas, all of you have become foremost.
Now, O heroes, a gift of treasure has appeared for you who serve the mortal worshipper;
drink, O Vājas, O Ṛbhus! We have offered to you the great third libation for exhilaration.
O Vājas, come hither to us, O Ṛbhukṣans, you great heroes who are praised for your wealth!
May your draughts come at the closing of the days; these [songs] have gone to you as cows go to their stall.
O sons of strength, come to this sacrifice, being invoked with reverence;
O wise ones, being of one mind, drink of this honeyed draught for which you are present, bestowing treasures along with Indra.
O Indra, being of one accord with Varuṇa, drink the Soma; being of one accord, O lover of songs, drink it with the Maruts.
Being of one accord with those who drink first and those who drink at the appointed seasons, being of one accord with the divine wives who bestow treasures—drink in harmony with them all.
In harmony with the Ādityas, rejoice; in harmony with the mountains, O Ṛbhus;
in harmony with the divine Savitṛ, in harmony with the rivers that bestow treasures.

Those R̥bhus who [strengthened] the Aśvins, those who [strengthened] their parents, and who by their aid fashioned the milch-cow, the two horses, the armor, and the two worlds; those far-reaching heroes who have performed noble deeds.

O *Ṛbhus*, you who bestow wealth consisting of cattle, booty, and brave sons— wealth rich in treasures and abundant in food— being exhilarated, grant that to us, O drinkers of the first draught, and to those who praise your gift.
You were not absent, nor did we fail to satisfy you; O Ṛbhus, you have been praised at this sacrifice.
Rejoice with Indra, with the Maruts, and with the kings, O gods, for the bestowing of treasures.
Come hither, O sons of Śavas, O R̥bhus, sons of Sudhanvan; do not stay away!
For at this libation of yours is the bestowing of treasures; may your exhilarations follow after Indra.
The gift of treasure from the Ṛbhus has arrived here; there has been the drinking of the well-pressed Soma, since by your skillful work and your dexterity you fashioned the single chalice into four.
"You have fashioned the chalice into four parts," he said, "O friend, teach us how! Then, O Vājas, you Ṛbhus with skillful hands reached the path of immortality, the assembly of the gods.
Of what material was this ladle made, which you fashioned into four by your wisdom?
Now press the juice for the exhilaration of the libation; drink, O Ṛbhus, of the honeyed Soma.
By your skillful power you made your parents young again; by your skillful power you fashioned the chalice for the drinking of the gods.
By your skillful power, O Ṛbhus, possessors of the treasure of booty, you wrought the two bay steeds that carry Indra and win the prize.
O Vājās, for him who presses for you at the close of days this sharp libation for exhilaration,
O Ṛbhus, you strong ones, being exhilarated, fashion for him wealth consisting of all heroic sons.
O Lord of the Bay Horses, you drank the pressed juice in the morning; the midday libation is yours alone.
Drink now together with the *Ṛbhus*, the bestowers of treasures—those whom you, O Indra, have made your friends through their skillful deeds.
O gods who have become perfected through holy works, who sit upon the heaven like falcons—bestow wealth upon us, O sons of strength! O sons of Sudhanvan, you have become immortal.

O Ṛbhus, you who are deft-handed and skillful, that third libation which you fashioned as a bestowal of treasure—that has been poured out for you; drink it together with exhilarating draughts that grant Indra-like power.
Born without horses and without reins, the praiseworthy three-wheeled chariot rolls around the realm.
O Ṛbhus, that proclamation of your divine power is great, in that you nourish both heaven and earth.

O Vājas and Ṛbhus, you of keen insight who by the meditation of your mind fashioned from thought a well-rolling chariot that does not waver—those of yours we now announce for the drinking of this libation. We call upon you.
O Vājas, O Ṛbhus, that greatness of yours has become well-proclaimed among the gods, O Vibhūs;
for you have fashioned your aged parents, worn out by time, into young men again so that they may move about.
You made the single chalice fourfold; by your insights, you brought forth the cow from the hide.
Then, through your readiness, O Vājas and Ṛbhus, you attained immortality among the gods—this deed of yours is worthy of praise.
From the *Ṛbhus* comes wealth most renowned, which the heroes, famed for their vigor, have generated;
fashioned by *Vibhvan*, it is to be proclaimed at the assemblies—he whom you gods protect is preeminent among men.
He is the prize-winning steed; he is the seer through his eloquence; he is the hero, the archer, invincible in battles.
He possesses the increase of wealth and true heroic might—he whom Vāja, Vibhvan, and the Ṛbhus have favored.
The most excellent and beautiful ornament has been placed upon you; O Vājas and Ṛbhus, take pleasure in this hymn of praise.
For you are wise, seers, and possessed of inspired insight; as such, we make ourselves known to you with this sacred prayer.
From the prayers of our thoughts, you who are wise, [bestow] all nourishments beneficial to men;
O *Ṛbhus*, fashion for us resplendent strength, most excellent vigor with bull-like power, and wealth and vitality.
Bestowing upon us offspring here and wealth here, fashion for us a fame accompanied by heroes;
O Ṛbhus, grant us that wonderful prize by which we may distinguish ourselves above others.
O Vājas, Ṛbhukṣans, and gods, come to our sacrifice by the paths traveled by the gods,
so that you, O joyous ones, may establish the sacrifice among these human clans on the auspicious days of the year.

May these sacrifices be pleasing to your heart and mind; may they, adorned with clarified butter, go forth today as offerings you enjoy. May the pressed juices, full to the brim, flow toward you; when drunk, may they exhilarate you for wisdom and skill.
O Vājas, O Ṛbhukṣans, just as this threefold rising praise, ordained by the gods, has been offered to you,
so have I, like Manu, poured out Soma among the later clans who dwell in the high heavens, in your company.
O you with fat horses, with radiant chariots, with iron helmets, powerful ones adorned with fine golden ornaments—
you, O sons of Indra, grandsons of strength— your foremost [drink] has been proclaimed for your exhilaration.
O Ṛbhukṣans, we invoke Ṛbhu— the wealth, the most powerful ally in the contest for booty— who is accompanied by Indra, who is ever most victorious, and who possesses the Aśvins.
O Ṛbhus, that mortal whom you and Indra protect— may he be a winner through his inspired thoughts at the winning of the prize, and may he be successful with his steed.
O Vājas, O R̥bhukṣans, find for us the paths so that we may sacrifice;
O wise ones, being praised, enable us to cross over all directions.
O Vājas, O Ṛbhukṣans, O Indra, O Nāsatyas, bestow upon us that wealth and horses from among the people; bestow it abundantly for the granting of riches.
For indeed, yours are those ancient gifts which Trasadasyu bestowed upon the Pūrus;
you two granted him mastery over fields and fertile lands, a fierce and overwhelming blow against the Dasyus.
And you two have indeed bestowed Dadhikrā, the prize-winner who overcomes many, who belongs to all people—
the swift, straight-flying eagle, dappled and fleet, worthy of praise like a noble king, a hero.
Whom all the people, exulting, rejoice at as he rushes forth like a torrent—
him who is eager for the prize like a hero seeking wisdom, who outstrips chariots with his feet and speeds along like the wind.

He who, obstructing the foe in battles, moves forward as a conqueror while seeking cattle; manifest and straight-acting, he has observed the sacrificial assemblies, passing beyond the obstruction of the mortal man.
And indeed, the people cry out after him in battles as if after a thief who steals a garment;
he who stoops low like a weary falcon, [driving] toward glory and toward a herd of cattle.
And as he is about to race among us for the first time, he stirs himself with the rows of chariots;
like a handsome suitor preparing his garland, he licks up the dust, tossing up the spray as he gallops.
And this prize-winning steed, victorious, faithful to the cosmic order, listening with his whole body in the battle,
